what_went_wrong: Invented revenues and margins, then precise NPVs/IRRs, despite 'directional estimates, not exact calculations'
rationale: The task said 'directional estimates, not exact calculations', and the reference gives no revenue figures. Opus invented revenue and margin inputs and reported precise NPVs and IRRs; the expert's report stays directional. Mode I: an explicit instruction was broken; secondary mode C, too precise for the evidence. Send back: the recommendation rests on invented numbers. D2. I added the 9% NPV item to this root cause (disagreement 7).

what_went_wrong: Dropdowns not uniform: the Regional tab offers regions, not a branch or the company; Ranking has no company-wide option
rationale: The task says all schedules should have a dropdown for a branch or the company total. Tabs 1, 2 and 5 have it. The Regional tab's selector lists Regions A to G and drives only the selected-region block, not the main table. The Ranking tab's selector lists the 10 branches with no company option; it drives a selected-branch scorecard shown beside the company figures. The Cover's how-to line says each report tab offers the branch-or-company choice, although its own tab index lists the two different selectors. An explicit instruction is broken on two of five tabs, so it counts even though this task has no expert file. Mode I. Send back: a supervisor would return a workbook whose cover misdescribes its controls. Haiku's matching row (H-F-2) is minor because it misses the instruction on one tab and says so; gpt-6.1-sol's workbook has one branch-or-company selector on all five tabs, so the instruction could be met. D1. Both first-pass reviewers agreed; re-read on 2026-11-11.

what_went_wrong: Regional view has EBITDA % but no gross margin % or SG&A %, so regions of different size are hard to compare
rationale: The task wants regions compared for senior management. Regions differ in size, so percentages are needed for a fair comparison, and Opus added EBITDA % but not gross margin % or SG&A %. This is substance a professional would include (decision rule 3). There is no expert file for this task. Mode P. Minor. D1. I decided this (disagreement 9), first as a rubric error and then corrected for consistency.

what_went_wrong: California-law section doesn't say why California law applies to YouTube or offer the do-not-sell option (the expert memo has both)

rationale: The task asked whether California law was violated and for the client's legal options. The memo doesn't say why California law applies to YouTube and doesn't offer the 'do not sell or share' option; the expert's memo has both (decision rule 4). Mode P. Minor. D1. what_went_wrong: SAR narrative has no per-account summary by transaction category with count, minimum, maximum and total
rationale: Section 3 gives selected counts and totals, mostly for Account 6, merges Accounts 1-2 and 4-5, and gives no minimum or maximum amounts. The workbook's Account Summary sheet has totals and counts by category but no min/max, and the item asks for the narrative. The expert's SAR lists all seven accounts by category with count, range and total. Mode P; minor; D1. Same reading as H-C-12 and S-C-9.

what_went_wrong: Will's personal-effects memo clause softened to 'may consider ... not binding'
rationale: The rubric expects the will to request that a personal-effects memorandum be honored. The will says the executor 'may consider' it and that it is 'not binding', which is a softened commitment (hand-check rule 2). A non-binding request to honor it would have satisfied this and the sole-discretion instruction together. There is no expert file for this task. Mode C: too hedged. Minor: a one-sentence edit, and the clause is legally accurate. gpt-6.1-sol's clause ('advisory only', S-L-18) has the same legal effect and carries the same severity; the severity was changed from send back on 2026-11-11. D2. I decided this (disagreement 4; hand-check row 25).

what_went_wrong: Legal jargon ('injunctions') left unexplained despite the plain-language instruction
rationale: The task required plain language suitable for a client. 'Injunctions' is used without explanation. It breaks an explicit instruction. Mode I. Minor. D1. Both reviewers agreed.

what_went_wrong: Two dollar formats mixed across the workbook
rationale: The workbook mixes two dollar formats: plain numbers with a '($)' label, and numbers with a $ sign. That is an objective inconsistency (hand-check row 22). Mode A. Minor. D1. Both reviewers agreed.

what_went_wrong: SAR calls Tavery the owner and 100% beneficial owner of Bluehaven but never says he manages it
rationale: The task says the Bluehaven account is 'owned and managed by Owen Tavery'. The SAR says 'its owner Owen Tavery' and '100% beneficial owner of Bluehaven' and nowhere gives the manager role. The expert's SAR says 'owned and managed by Owen Tavery', so decision rule 4 makes the omission real. Mode P (a given fact left out, nothing wrong stated); minor; D1. Same reading as Haiku's first-run row H-C-10.

what_went_wrong: No representation that NoxaPulse is solvent
rationale: Article III has 24 Company representations, including no undisclosed liabilities and no Indebtedness (3.11), but none on solvency. The expert's agreement says 'The Company is not insolvent' and the task asked for customary representations, so decision rule 4 makes it real. Mode P; minor; D1.

what_went_wrong: Sources appendix gives publisher, date and topic but no URL for any source and no title for several
basis: fresh (first-run F-K1 was E4; web tools were available this time)
rationale: Page 13 lists entries such as 'Mirae Asset Securities (29-Nov-2023)', 'Consumer Insight (4-Mar-2024)' and 'InvestChosun (7-Apr-2024)' with neither title nor URL; no entry has a URL. The run made 18 web searches, so the titles and links were in hand; the first-run excuse (no internet) no longer applies. Mode P; minor; D1.

what_went_wrong: Loosened legal standards: COPPA 'knew (or should have known)'; CCPA suits 'only for data breaches'
rationale: Two legal standards are stated loosely: COPPA's knowledge test as 'knew (or should have known)', and CCPA private suits as 'only for data breaches'. The rubric items still passed (hand-check rows 9 and 19), so no points were lost. It is recorded because a loose statement of a legal rule is an objective error. Mode K. Minor. D2.

what_went_wrong: 16 summary cells display ####### in Excel (column too narrow)
basis: hand-check row 29 (item passed; verified in Excel)
rationale: 16 cells in the reconciliation summaries display ####### in Excel because one column is too narrow. It is an objective display defect, verified in Excel. The overall-formatting item still passed (hand-check row 29), so no points were lost. Mode A. Minor. D1.

what_went_wrong: Rubric and expert wage rates are above the contract excerpt given to the model ($1.00 on each per-service and hourly rate, $7.98 on the weekly guarantee)
rationale: The contract excerpt given to the model has $251.06 per service, a $2,008.50 weekly guarantee, $55.67 per rehearsal hour and $76.59 / $137.87 for 1- and 2-hour sound checks. The expert's file and the rubric use $252.06, $2,016.48, $56.67, $77.59 and $138.87: each per-service or hourly rate is $1.00 higher, and the weekly guarantee is $7.98 higher (2,016.48 is 8 x 252.06). Opus used the source's rates and matches the expert's method at those rates. Recomputed with part2/scripts/theatre_recompute.py.

what_went_wrong: Doubling pay computed on scale wages, not compounded on the premium (contract is silent)
rationale: The contract says only '25% additional pay' and gives no base. Opus applied the right tiers to scale wages and disclosed the choice; the expert compounds doubling on the premium. Both readings fit the text.

what_went_wrong: Rubric enforces the expert's EOR/MIR IDs, two named tabs and a Testing Type column against the task's SCRA-12a to SCRA-18 IDs
rationale: The task prescribes the IDs SCRA-12a to 12d and SCRA-13 to 18 and asks for no tabs or type column. Opus's new file uses exactly those IDs (Test Questions A6:A15), with s3937 citations on 12a-d and s3919 citations on 13-18. The rubric contradicts the task (decision rule 3).

what_went_wrong: Rubric's variance sign contradicts the task's sign rule
rationale: The task says a cost increase must show as negative. Costs are positive numbers in the data, so the rubric's literal 'M24 minus M23' would show an increase as positive. The rubric contradicts the task and its own sign items; Opus followed the task.

what_went_wrong: Rubric wants citations on topics 1-5 and 11; the task asks for them on 6-10 only
rationale: The task scopes citations to topics 6 to 10, and Opus cited exactly those. The rubric penalises following an explicit scope set by the task. This differs from F-B4, which is real: there the task said nothing about margin percentages and the comparison needs them, while here the task itself says where the citations go.

what_went_wrong: Rubric's Schedule A line 5a ($2,246) is the state table amount only; Opus added the local sales tax the IRS worksheet requires ($719), so lines 5a, 12, 15, 16, 24 and 37 differ
rationale: The 2024 IRS table gives $2,246 for Texas, income $300,000+, family of 5, and the Texas footnote says to add local sales tax by the ratio method. Opus used $2,246 + $2,246 x 2.00/6.25 = $2,965 and disclosed the 2% San Antonio rate as an assumption. The expert's Schedule A stops at the state amount, so the rubric's six figures are $719 of deduction (about $173 of tax) away from the IRS method. Close to E5 because the local rate is an assumption; see Doubts.

what_went_wrong: Source's single 'Other Costs' block split between Tour and Travel differently from the rubric
rationale: The source has a single 'Other Costs' block, so the tour/travel split is a judgement. Opus disclosed its split; totals and net income are unchanged. The number differs from the rubric's, so the item itself fails (hand-check row 36).

what_went_wrong: Substitute-synthesizer pay clause read differently from the expert
rationale: The substitute-synthesizer clause is ambiguous. Opus's reading (150% per show plus a 25% premium) is closer to the literal text than the expert's.

what_went_wrong: Rubric names a different platform and law firm from the task (VueVid / Sullivan Bryson)
rationale: The rubric names VueVid and Sullivan Bryson; the task says YouTube and X Privacy Law. On content, each of the seven items is met. One of the seven items (18aa4bc1) is also loosely drawn on the law: it says the CCPA may be violated 'by collecting' without consent, while the statute's consent rule for minors is about sale and sharing.

what_went_wrong: Rubric requires content the source file doesn't contain (names, benefits, tax exclusions)
rationale: The reference file has no names, instruments, benefits or tax exclusions, so the rubric's content can't be produced from the inputs. Opus copied all 103 roster rows exactly.

what_went_wrong: Reported the trial balance as provided and proposed the write-off; the expert booked it
rationale: The task says to flag issues and notify the CFO before finalising. Opus reported the trial balance as provided and proposed the same write-off entry that the expert booked.

what_went_wrong: Rubric expects a phantom $1 of Additional Medicare Tax withholding (Form 8959 lines 19 and 24, Form 1040 line 25c)
expert_meets_item: n/a (expert is the source of the $1)
rationale: The three W-2 box 6 amounts sum to $5,124.43, exactly 1.45% of Medicare wages, so nothing extra was withheld. The expert's 5,125 and $1 come from rounding each W-2 before adding. Opus shows 5,124, 0 and 0, which is correct.

what_went_wrong: Fairness opinion only to be considered; the expert memo never mentions one
basis: expert rule; hand-check row 35 (item not met)
rationale: The rubric item is not met: 'consider a fairness opinion' is a softened commitment (hand-check row 35). But the expert's memo never mentions a fairness opinion at all, so this is not a gap against the expert (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: Inserted a helper column so the task's column letters line up (task contradicts the file)
rationale: The task's column letters contradict the source file. Opus added a helper column so the task's letters line up; all 65 sampled rows match the source. A helper column at the end would have been cleaner.

what_went_wrong: Corporate SG&A kept as a separate reconciling column
rationale: The source data puts Corporate in its own region with no revenue, $13.9M of SG&A and all $10.1M of shared-service allocations in FY2024. Regions A to G can equal the company total only if Corporate's costs are spread across regions, which the task does not ask for. Opus spread the allocations by revenue and kept Corporate SG&A in its own column so that regions plus Corporate reconcile to the total, and says so on the Cover and the tab. The item could be met by a different allocation choice, so this is a defensible alternative, not a rubric error.

what_went_wrong: No roadmap, 'how to proceed', statement of support or sign-off (not asked for by the task)
rationale: A roadmap sentence, a 'how do you wish to proceed' line, a statement of support and a sign-off are style conventions taken from the expert's memo. The task asked for none of them (decision rule 3, style). I decided the roadmap item (disagreement 8); the other three are the same kind. The expert's memo has all four. That does not make them real: decision rule 4 says a gap counts only if the expert has the element, not that everything the expert has counts, and these four are closing conventions of a letter (decision rule 3).

what_went_wrong: Bob's short-term sale reported directly on Schedule D line 1a, with no Form 8949 Part I, where the rubric expects Form 8949 Box A and line 1b
rationale: Both items are not met as written: line 1b is blank and Form 8949 has no short-term page. The official Schedule D and Form 8949 both say a covered sale with no adjustments may go straight to line 1a, and Bob's 1099-B has box 12 checked and no box 1g amount. Opus disclosed the choice in a note on Form 8949 and the loss of $6,694 is right. The expert used the other permitted route.

what_went_wrong: Neither memo defines personal information under the CCPA or works through sale/sharing
rationale: The expert's memo, like Opus's, gives only the opt-in rule for minors. Neither defines personal information under the CCPA or works through sale and sharing (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: Neither memo says the minority vote excludes the controller's affiliates
rationale: Neither memo says the minority vote excludes the controller's affiliates; the expert says only that the controller abstains (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: Judged projects at a self-chosen 12% hurdle instead of the given 9% WACC
rationale: The task states the 9% WACC as a fact, not as the rate to use. Adding a disclosed risk premium for riskier projects is common practice. The missing 9% view of Project B is already counted under F-P2, so counting it here would double count. I decided this (table review 5).

what_went_wrong: States the controller's duty of care (gross negligence) from Sears but never applies it to Marcus's refusal; says care-based theories against Marcus fail under the controller exculpation in DGCL s144(d)(5)
rationale: Item not met: the memo never says the refusal can be gross negligence. The memo gives a stated reason: a 2025 statute bars money damages against a controller for care breaches, so it frames the claim as loyalty or bad faith. The statute text was checked and reads as the memo says. The first-run memo had no such reasoning, so the first-run ruling (L-R14, real) is not repeated. Close call; see Doubts.

what_went_wrong: Two extra details the expert memo also omits (COPPA internal-operations exception, 45-day response timeline)
rationale: The expert's memo also omits the COPPA internal-operations exception and the 45-day response timeline, and the task did not ask for either. Neither file meets the two items (decision rule 4). Classed E5 at table review 6, before the expert rule existed; moved to E6 on 2026-11-11, because an item the expert's file also misses is E6.

what_went_wrong: Rubric says columns G and H hold Q2 then Q3; the source file and the expert's file have Q3 then Q2
rationale: The item says columns G and H on the first worksheet hold Q2 2024 and Q3 2024, 'consistent with the Population reference column positions'. The Population file has Q3 in G and Q2 in H, and so does the expert's own Sample file; both judges failed the expert's file on this item. The judge read the item correctly and the item contradicts the source, so this is a rubric error, not a judge error. Opus's quarter values match the Population on all 65 rows. Split out of the judge-error row A-J on 2026-11-11.

what_went_wrong: Rubric's AP items need AP_TB-1.xlsx, which the dataset doesn't include; Opus flagged it
rationale: The task names AP_TB-1.xlsx, but the dataset doesn't contain it. Opus marked the schedule as pending and raised it as its first high-priority flag.

expert_meets_item: no, for a different reason (no date clipping); its day count is exclusive
rationale: Opus counts both the start and end day and discloses it. The largest difference from the rubric's formula is 0.076 percentage points, and both methods flag the same 53 awards.

what_went_wrong: 21-year trust cap measured from the testator's death
rationale: The will follows the task's 'maximum trust duration of 21 years' literally, measured from the testator's death.

what_went_wrong: Roster linked by numbered slot position rather than an ID lookup; the expert's roster has no ID at all
expert_meets_item: no (roster has name and instrument only)
rationale: The numbered roster slots act as the unique ID on the Roster, Payroll and Schedule tabs. The expert's file has no musician ID, and the task doesn't ask for one. I decided this (disagreement 6). The expert's roster holds a name and an instrument and no identifier, so neither file meets the item; the class moved from E5 to E6 on 2026-11-11 (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: A rehearsal under 3 hours is paid at the 3-hour minimum call and noted, not flagged as a conflict; over 5 consecutive hours is flagged
rationale: The contract sets a 3-hour minimum call (7.1) and bars more than 5 consecutive hours without a meal break (7.5); it has no per-day totals. The expert's file marks any rehearsal row under 3 or over 5 hours as CHECK and pays the hours entered. Opus pays the 3-hour minimum, writes '3-hour minimum call applied (Art. 7.1)' on the row, and marks more than 5 consecutive hours without a meal break as a violation. Both files deal with a short rehearsal; they differ on whether it is a conflict or a pay rule. Opus's reading follows the contract's wording and is stated in its Instructions, so the element is handled differently, not missing, and decision rule 4 does not reach it.

what_went_wrong: Order growth measured on units rather than dollars
rationale: The task says 'order growth' without saying units or dollars. Opus uses units and shows dollars as a memo; the branch ranking is identical either way.

what_went_wrong: No complete totals and counts per subject in the SAR; the expert's SAR has none either
rationale: The SAR gives figures by account and by red flag, not a total and count for each of the four subjects. The expert's SAR is organised by account and has no per-subject totals (file read). Decision rule 4: shared with the expert.

what_went_wrong: Suspicious amount stated as $2,868,190.08 (all credits), with debits of $1,691,476.42 shown beside it; the rubric wants $4,559,667 (credits plus debits)
rationale: Not met as written (grading rule 7). The SAR's figure is correct against the source (742 credits), it states the basis ('all credits to the subject accounts') and gives the debit total, and the two sum to the rubric's $4,559,666.50. Counting money in and the same money out is disputable. Same reading as H-C-14 and S-C-8.

what_went_wrong: No FTC press-release link (no internet; the case is cited with its docket number)
rationale: Opus couldn't open or verify a web address, and a link recalled from memory could be wrong. The case is identified by name, amount and court docket number. I decided this (table review 6).

what_went_wrong: Neither model lets a musician be added without extending fixed-range formulas
rationale: Both models use fixed-range totals and no Excel tables, so adding a musician means extending formulas in either. The expert's file was opened to confirm (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: No conditional formatting on variances (not asked for; negatives already show in red)
rationale: The task never asks for conditional formatting. Negative variances already show in red through the number format. It is a presentation choice. I decided this (table review 2).

what_went_wrong: Rubric's legal balance copies a double count in the source file; Opus used the correct GL figure
rationale: The source file's total sums a subtotal twice (L62 includes L60). The trial balance confirms 435,284.69, which Opus reported while flagging the bug. The rubric and the expert carry the doubled figure.

what_went_wrong: Rubric expects an arbitration discussion; YouTube's terms have no arbitration clause
rationale: YouTube's real terms have no arbitration clause or class waiver (checked against the published terms). The item fits the rubric's other platform, and the memo describes the forum clause correctly.

what_went_wrong: Consistent accounting format without $ (same as the expert's file)
rationale: The amounts use one consistent accounting format without a $ sign. The expert's file uses the same style, and the task doesn't ask for $ signs. I decided this (disagreement 5). The expert's file does not meet the item either, so the class moved from E5 to E6 on 2026-11-11 (decision rule 4).

what_went_wrong: Income statement ends at EBIT (data has no interest or tax)
rationale: The data has no interest or tax accounts, so EBIT is the bottom line. The data has 21 accounts and none is interest or tax; a net income line could only repeat EBIT under another name.

what_went_wrong: 'March' appears in comparison columns and source rows; the expert's bonus tab carries the same 'March' rows
expert_meets_item: no (same 'March' rows on the bonus tab)
rationale: The 'March' strings are a deliberate comparison column, the source file's own 'March accrual' and 'March reverse' rows on the bonus tab, and the change log the task asked for; none is a stale period label. The expert's bonus tab carries the same two 'March' rows, so the expert's file does not meet the item either (decision rule 4). Moved from E5 to E6 on 2026-11-11.

what_went_wrong: Pre-emptive right is capped at the Pro Rata Share but a bracketed sentence lets the Investor take up shares other rights-holders decline
rationale: Section 9.3 caps the right at 'his Pro Rata Share' and then adds, in brackets, an over-allotment over securities that 'any other holder ... having a similar right' does not buy. That is not a firm cap (grading rule 2), so the item is not met as written. It is an optional, pro-client addition of a common kind, flagged for the client by the brackets; the rubric's cap is a limit on the client that the task did not ask for.

what_went_wrong: No s3937 question states the 'not materially affected' court-relief standard
rationale: SCRA-12a says 'unless a court granted the servicer relief under s3937(c)' and its guidance cells require a court order for an ability-to-pay refusal, but the 'not materially affected by military service' finding appears only on the Statutory Text sheet (B11). The expert's questions do not mention court relief at all (decision rule 4).
